## Notes

... sympathetic characters also refuse to name Stephen, Puddle say, 'just because you are what you are...' And although Stephen's cry of, 'why am I am as I am - and what am I?' is apparently resolved, she still refrains from using sexological labels, or any labels at all. When meeting Valérie Seymour, Stephen fears that Valérie 'liked her because she thought me - oh, well, because she thought me what I am.' Stephen never refers to herself as an invert or as a lesbian.

### P.9

... For these two were strangely shy with each other. - it was almost grotesque, this shyness of theirs, as existing between mother and child. ... Stephen, acutely responsive to beauty, would be dimly longing to find expression for a feeling almost amounting to worship, that her mother's face has awakened. But Anna, looking gravely at her daughter, noting the plentiful auburn hair, the brave hazel eyes that were so like the father's, as indeed were the child's whole expression and bearing, would be filled with a sudden antagonism that came very near to anger.

She would lie awake at night and ponder this thing, scourging herself in an access of contrition, accusing herself of hardness of spirit, of being an unnatural mother. Sometimes she would shed slow, miserable tears, remembering the inarticulate Stephen.

Sometimes Stephen pictured them living alone in a low thatched cottage, by the side of a mill stream — she had seen such a cottage not very far from Upton — and the water flowed quickly and made talking noises. ...

In this picture it was Collins who talked about loving, and Stephen who gently but firmly rebuked her. 'There, there, Collins, don't be silly, you are a queer fish!' And yet all the while she would be longing to tell her how wonderful it was, ...

### P.65

... But now, here she was, very wishful to pray, while not knowing how to explain her dilemma: 'I'm terribly unhappy, dear, improbable God' — would not be a very propitious beginning. And yet at this moment she was wanting a God and a tangible one, very kind and paternal, a God with a white flowing beard and wide forehead, a benevolent parent who would lean out of Heaven and turn His face sideways the better to listen from His cloud, upheld by cherubs and angels. ...

It was fear that aroused their antagonism; in her they instinctively sensed an outlaw, and theirs was the task of policing nature.

Outrageous, Puddle would feel it to be, that wilfully selfish tyranny of silence evolved by a crafty old ostrich of a world for its own well-being and comfort. The world hid its head in the sands of convention, so that seeing nothing it might avoid Truth. It said to itself: 'If seeing's believing, then I don't want to see — if silence is golden, it is also, in this case, very expedient.' There were moments when Puddle would feel sorely tempted to shout out loud at the world. ...

# MCP servers had a rough 48 hours: 4 unauthenticated CVEs

## Thesis

多个 MCP 服务器把工具接口裸奔上网, 认证缺失是系统性问题

## Notes

- 4 个 MCP 服务器的 HTTP/SSE 工具接口没设认证, 谁都能连 (CVSS 9.8/10.0)
- GitLab Workhorse 那个最狠: 工具调用能把服务器环境变量读出来 -- 字符串越过信任边界
- LiteLLM: 有认证检查, 但任意 Bearer token 都被当成合法 (假锁), 已确认被利用, 进了 CISA KEV
- CVE = 漏洞身份证号; CVSS = 严重程度打分; KEV = 正在被利用名单
- 研究连接: 没认证 = 系统不知道用户是谁 = 同意(consent)无处可挂, 同意机制直接失效

# Antitrust Economics at a time of upheaval: Chp14 The German Facebook Case

## Thesis

Facebook's supra-competitive data collection = abuse of dominance, equivalent to excessive pricing in a zero-price market

## Notes

- EU vs US: lack of post-Chicago analysis in EU cases; in Europe competition law is lawyers' realm
- Dominance: attention market - companies compete for user attention; active users determine dominance; user becomes the product
- Abuse / as-if competition: would yield social networks not requiring WhatsApp+Instagram data linkage
- Facebook zero-cost; supra-competitive data collection and usage = excessive pricing, enforceable only via dominant position
- Benchmarks for excess: price difference? profit margins? FCO: abuse = not respecting rules protecting consumers in unbalanced bargaining position
- super-profiles = quality deterioration = price increase in zero-price market
- harm starts when one market side imposes rules on the other ('take-it-or-leave-it'); FCO: consumers empowered vs dominant firms is prerequisite for competitive process
- competitors at disadvantage if they respected GDPR
- FCO ruling: bundling social network + massive personalized data collection; Hayekian: markets are decentralized info systems, competition needs meaningful options; giant data reservoir = entry barrier; consumers pay via data exploitation harm
- pros for users: efficiency. cons: data leaking; data collection may make users change behavior to please others/public bodies

# Q25: Is my bad work ethic linked to "the stickiness" of my behavior? How to solve it?

## My Symptoms

1. 很难进入工作，一天内要么什么都不做，要么只做一件事。
2. 一旦开始了一件事，就容易停不下来，而其它事则更难开始。

## Solutions

### Implementation intention

- Definition (Webb & Sheeran, 2007): implementation intentions are plans that specify when, where, and how of goal striving in advance.
- "Implementation intention forges an association between that cue and a response that is instrumental for obtaining one's goal."
- How it works: implementation intention effects were mediated by the accessibility of the specified cue and by the strength of cue-response links. That is, a mental link is formed between the if component and the then component of the plan.

### Cues

- Altman & Trafton (2004): when you return, relevant cues — such as the task interface or information about your previous work — help you retrieve the task's context from memory, which leads to faster resumption.

# Defaults and the having-to-explain friction

## Question

Is part of the cost of opting out of a default the cost of having to explain yourself — i.e., exiting the shared common ground that the default provides?

## Why it matters

The consent-architecture cost model (professor's frame: information acquisition vs. toggle-switching) may be missing a third cost: leaving a default ([[hub-privacy]]) means leaving common ground, and the system taxes the leaver in explanations. "Are you sure?" opt-out dialogs are the platform demanding an explanation from the non-default choice. The default user is legible without explaining; the opt-out user must justify herself to keep going. Paragraph for the narrative section on defaults and costly attention.

## Next

Read one anchor: Garfinkel's breaching experiments (shortest path to the mechanism).

## Notes

- Her example (2026-10-18): same school as a kid — "the purple book, p.151" needs zero explanation because the default (same classes, schedule, teachers) is shared. As adults meeting after five years apart, every reference needs grounding work first: why I'm doing this, why now, why these people. Defaults = institutionalized common ground: legal defaults (forms, documents) and cultural defaults decide who never has to explain.
- Theory anchors:
  - **Herbert Clark — common ground** (*Using Language*, 1996): conversation as joint action; shared assumptions make reference cheap. The school example is literally this.
  - **Harold Garfinkel — breaching experiments** (*Studies in Ethnomethodology*, 1967): subjects instructed to act as if common ground didn't exist produced exactly "having to explain everything," met with bewilderment and anger. Direct empirical demo of the friction.
  - **Bourdieu — doxa** (*Outline of a Theory of Practice*, 1977): the taken-for-granted that "goes without saying"; doxa never explains, only heterodoxy must argue. The philosophical version of defaults.
  - **James Scott — legibility** (*Seeing Like a State*, 1998): the default position is the legible one; non-defaults must render themselves legible — i.e., explain.
  - **Thaler & Sunstein — choice architecture** (*Nudge*, 2008); **Johnson, Bellman & Lohse (2002)** on privacy defaults: the econ baseline for opt-in/opt-out stickiness (already in reading list 7.0).
  - **Coase/Williamson — transaction costs**: explanation as the transaction cost of deviating from the institutional default; the econ-language version of the same claim.

# Is earning money actually the value you generate, or is it just the result of a game you participate in?

## How this question is formed

- Being a buyer and a seller feels like a performance, not something natural.
- Money feels like a prop (道具) in a game called economics.
- People spend money because they have money; if they didn't, they'd only buy necessary goods, not interesting things.
- You depend on others to produce interesting goods for you, and you pay them money — basically to keep playing the game.
- Becoming an adult, becoming a businessman, feels magical: how do you earn money? Somehow you just earn it.
- Earning money doesn't feel like the value you generated — it feels like the result of a game you participated in.
- To earn money you have to perform: make people believe you have value — as if you already have money — in order to earn money.
- The other side of the same performance: people feel they have to spend money because they have it, so they give it to you.
- You can end up with a product that has no use whatsoever — and the exchange still happens through the performance.

# Ellison IO Lecture Notes

## Contents

- [Single Product Monopoly Pricing](#single-product-monopoly-pricing)
- [Monopoly and Product Quality](#monopoly-and-product-quality)
- [Multiple Product Monopoly Pricing](#multiple-product-monopoly-pricing)
- [Durable Goods Monopoly](#durable-goods-monopoly)

Self-study notes. L01: Monopoly Pricing & Durable Goods, I — Glenn Ellison.

## Single Product Monopoly Pricing

$$\max_{x} P(x)x - C(x)$$

FOC:

$$\underbrace{P(x) + P'(x) \cdot x}_{MR} - C'(x) = 0$$

$$\Rightarrow \frac{P(x) - C'(x)}{P(x)} = -\frac{1}{\varepsilon}$$

where $\varepsilon$ is the price elasticity of demand at $p$, $\varepsilon = \frac{dx}{dp} \cdot \frac{p}{x}$.

**Lerner Index:** $\frac{P(x) - C'(x)}{P(x)}$ — the % of the product's price that is marked up above its marginal cost of production. A firm's ability to charge prices higher than what it costs to produce an additional unit without losing all its customers.

1) Never $|\varepsilon| < 1$: if $|\varepsilon| < 1$, then $-1/\varepsilon > 1$, but $(P - MC)/P$ will never exceed 1.

2) $\varepsilon = -100$, $|\varepsilon|$ big $\Rightarrow -1/\varepsilon = 1/100 \Rightarrow P \approx MC$.

## Monopoly and Product Quality

Quality $s \in \mathbb{R}$. Cost: $C(q, s) = q \cdot C(s)$.

Consumer preference $\theta \sim U[0, 1]$ (uniformly distributed).

If the firm sells $q$ units, it will sell to consumers with $\theta \in [1-q, 1]$. The indifferent consumer has $\theta = 1 - q$, for whom $p = v(s, 1-q)$.

Monopolist's problem:

$$\max_{q, s} q[v(s, 1-q) - C(s)]$$

FOC (with respect to quality):

$$\frac{\partial v}{\partial s}(s^m, 1-q^m) = \frac{\partial C}{\partial s}(s^m)$$

The effect of marginal cost spent is the benefit to the *marginal consumer*.

Social planner's problem:

$$\max_{q, s} \int_{1-q}^{1} (v(s, \theta) - C(s)) \, d\theta$$

FOC:

$$\frac{1}{q}\int_{1-q}^{1} \frac{\partial v}{\partial s}(s, \theta) \, d\theta = \frac{\partial C}{\partial s}(s)$$

The effect is the benefit to the *average consumer*.

## Multiple Product Monopoly Pricing

Demands $x_1(p_1, p_2)$, $x_2(p_1, p_2)$. Cost: $C(x_1, x_2) = c_1 x_1 + c_2 x_2$.

Monopolist's problem:

$$\max_{p_1, p_2} (p_1 - c_1)x_1(p_1, p_2) + (p_2 - c_2)x_2(p_1, p_2)$$

FOC:

$$(p_i - c_i)\frac{\partial x_i}{\partial p_i} + x_i(p_1, p_2) + (p_j - c_j)\frac{\partial x_j}{\partial p_i} = 0$$

Dividing by $\partial x_i / \partial p_i$:

$$(p_i - c_i) + \frac{x_i(p_1, p_2)}{\partial x_i / \partial p_i} + (p_j - c_j)\frac{\partial x_j / \partial p_i}{\partial x_i / \partial p_i} = 0$$

Markup formula:

$$\frac{p_i - c_i}{p_i} = -\frac{1}{\varepsilon_{ii}} - \frac{p_j - c_j}{p_i \cdot \partial x_i / \partial p_i} \cdot \frac{\partial x_j}{\partial p_i}$$

with $(p_j - c_j) > 0$, and $\partial x_j / \partial p_i > 0$ for substitutes, $< 0$ for complements.

Example noted on the page: newspapers and ads — ① the newspaper sells more; ② the ads are largely profitable.

## Durable Goods Monopoly

Two-period. $\theta \in [0, 1] \sim F(\theta)$.

Utility: $u = 2\theta - p_1$ if buy at $t = 1$; $u = \theta - p_2$ if buy at $t = 2$.

Cutoffs: types $\theta < \hat\theta_2$ don't buy; $\hat\theta_2 \le \theta < \hat\theta_1$ buy at $t = 2$; $\theta \ge \hat\theta_1$ buy at $t = 1$.

$p_2 = \hat\theta_2$. The marginal $t = 1$ buyer is indifferent between buying at $t = 1$ and waiting:

$$2\hat\theta_1 - p_1 = \hat\theta_1 - p_2 \Rightarrow p_1 = \hat\theta_1 + p_2 = \hat\theta_1 + \hat\theta_2$$

Monopolist's problem:

$$\max_{\hat\theta_2 \le \hat\theta_1} \Pi(\hat\theta_1, \hat\theta_2)$$

$$\Pi = (\hat\theta_1 + \hat\theta_2 - c)[1 - F(\hat\theta_1)] + (\hat\theta_2 - c)[F(\hat\theta_1) - F(\hat\theta_2)] = \hat\theta_1[1 - F(\hat\theta_1)] + (\hat\theta_2 - c)[1 - F(\hat\theta_2)]$$

$\Rightarrow$ Two separate monopoly pricing problems: one with $c_1 = 0$, one with $c_2 = c > 0$.

Since $c_1 (= 0) < c_2 (> 0) \Rightarrow MC_1 < MC_2$. With the price lower, the monopolist will dig deeper in the valuation (type) $\Rightarrow \hat\theta_1 < \hat\theta_2$. But $\hat\theta_1 \ge \hat\theta_2$ is given earlier, so $\hat\theta_1 = \hat\theta_2 \Rightarrow$ the monopoly only sells at $t = 1$.

- [ ] [YC — Y Combinator](https://www.youtube.com/@ycombinator) — startup，创始人和投资人的课
- [ ] [Perell — David Perell](https://www.youtube.com/@DavidPerellChannel) — writing online，How I Write

## 课

- [ ] [MIT film theory — The Film Experience](https://www.classcentral.com/course/mit-opencourseware-the-film-experience-fall-2013-40957) — David Thorburn，23 讲，免费，电影史 + 怎么看电影
